claims.text: Graphene nanoplatelets are pre-treated with a thin, stable interfacial coating, such as silicon carbide, before incorporation into a tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy.
Incorporating the coated graphene nanoplatelets will produce a coherent percolating network in the alloy.
The graphene network will enhance heat dissipation through graphene's intrinsically high thermal conductivity.
The interfacial coating will prevent carbide formation and minimize thermal mismatch at elevated temperatures.
The baseline is a tungsten-based refractory HEA, exemplified by WMoTaNb, produced by powder processing and spark plasma sintering without graphene.
The intervention introduces 1–3 vol% coated graphene nanoplatelets during powder processing and SPS densification.
The proposed effect is expected under cyclic thermal loading from 800 to 1200 °C combined with mechanical loading representative of plasma-facing conditions.
The coated graphene nanoplatelets will be well dispersed and form a nanoscale interconnected network along HEA grain boundaries.
The coated graphene network will have robust interfacial bonding and resist deleterious high-temperature reactions.
Continuous graphene pathways will rapidly dissipate thermal energy.
Interfacial stabilization will mitigate thermal-mismatch stresses and preserve mechanical integrity.
The intervention will increase effective thermal conductivity by approximately 50–70% relative to the graphene-free HEA baseline.
The modified material will maintain yield strength and ductility during high-temperature cyclic loading.
Benefits may be lost above 1200 °C because the interfacial coating may degrade or the graphene dispersion may become non-uniform.
Prolonged high-flux neutron irradiation may limit the benefits of the intervention.
Long-term coating stability and uniform graphene dispersion remain uncertain.

contradictions.description: Silicon carbide is offered as the coating while the coating is said to prevent carbide formation and clear evidence of carbide formation is a falsification condition. Without distinguishing the intentionally deposited SiC from newly formed reaction carbides, the criterion is internally ambiguous.

The predicted improvement and falsification threshold are relative to a graphene-free HEA baseline, but the experiment includes only untreated-graphene and coated-graphene samples. It therefore omits the stated baseline needed to evaluate the 50% improvement criterion.
